newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican helicopter market seen taking off.
newsitem.headline: Mexican helicopter market seen taking off.

text.p: Between the end of the Cold War and the Mexican economic crisis of 1995, the tight and highly competitive helicopter market took a nose dive in Mexico, according to manufacturers.
But the Mexican market has rebounded in a big way, bringing four major manufacturers into a new clash of the titans whose results have yet to be sorted out.

Bell Helicopter, Eurocopter, McDonnell Douglas Helicopter Systems and Sikorsky Aircraft Coporation all came to Acapulco over the weekend to make their pitch at Aeroexpo '97, a international aviation trade show and convention.

Representatives of all four helicopter makers told Reuters they have come to the same conclusion, that Mexico is the center of their attention in Latin America, with military, police and corporate clients back in the market.

"Mexico is the most important market in Latin America," said George Perez, Latin America sales manager for McDonnell Douglas Helicopter Systems, a subsidiary of McDonnell Douglas. "The private sector is growing significantly in Mexico, and that's the sector we want to expand into."

Bell Helicopter, a subsidiary of Textron Inc, and Eurocopter, a joint venture of France's Aerospatiale and Germany's Daimler-Benz Aerospace, account for nearly 90 percent of the world market, with Bell holding more than half the world market share, industry sources said.
But worldwide demand is only about 450 helicopters a year, and demand in Mexico is seen at about 20 units this year, said Art McAnarney, Bell's marketing director for Mexico.

Then last year, the United States announced it was giving Mexico 73 surplus military helicopters free of charge to help with the fight against the illegal narcotics traffic, 20 of which arrived last year with 53 due in 1997.
That came after Russia sold 12 of its old Soviet-made MI8 and MI17 helicopters to the Mexican Navy at rock-bottom prices.
"It was great until they started giving them away for free," McAnarney said.
Worse was the sudden Mexican peso devaluation of December 1994 that in 1995 caused Mexico's worst recession in decades. Eurocopter sold one helicopter in 1995. The others were shut out.

Still, the war on drugs in Mexico is expected to fuel demand in the police, military and government sectors. Plus, wealthy executives need helicopters to escape the Mexico City traffic and reach their private aircraft in the city of Toluca west of Mexico City, since non-commerical planes were banished from the Mexico City airport a few years ago.
Bell and Eurocopter offer a full line of helicopters, while McDonnell Douglas has its success in the small-helicopter sector and Sikorsky has done better with larger models.
The director general for Eurocopter de Mexico, Christian Gras, said his company did well to sell 10 units in 1996, eight of them to the state-owned oil company Pemex.
"There are strong needs for the for the petroleum industry here in Mexico and I really believe there are strong needs for police missions," Gras said.
Eurocopter also boasts of being the brand used by President Ernesto Zedillo. The Mexican presidency has nine Eurocopters.

McDonnell Douglas is trying to move into the market for medium-sized helicopters with a new technology that does away with the tail rotor, increasing ground safety and reducing noise at the same time, Perez said.
The MD-600 is the only helicopter allowed to fly in the Grand Canyon because of noise restrictions, he said.
Sikorsky is making a renewed push into Mexico and Latin America after backing off for several years, said Frederick W. Almeida, Sikorsky's business manager for Latin America.

Almeida said the company recently formed a seven-member marketing team to cover the region from Mexico to the southern cone of South America after having pulled out of Latin America in the 1980s when economies went sour, governments became more autocratic and loans were defaulted on.
Chilean Gen. Augusto Pinochet once rode in a Sikorsky, Almeida said.
But Bell is the clear market leader.
Of the estimated 450 to 470 helicopters in Mexico, 350 to 360 of them are Bell, McAnarney said.

"It's a very competitive market. All the manufacturers are very competitive in performance and cost," he said. "Our edge comes in after-market support with free technical advice, availability of spare parts, and training."
((--Mexico City newsroom, +728-9507))
